context: The “Input board heights” table below gives the height array, indexed from 0. At the initial endpoints [0, 7], the heights are 3 and 4. The left board is shorter, and the capacity is min(3, 4) × 7 = 21.
Container capacity is cap[i, j] = min(ht[i], ht[j]) × (j - i). The shorter board sets the water height, and the difference between the indices gives the width.
description: The top row shows cap[0, 7] → cap[1, 7] with a right-pointing arrow labeled “Move from the shorter board.” Below, a bracket labeled “Skipped states” spans six diagrams in two rows of three. Reading each row from left to right, i stays at 0 while j takes the values 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, and 1.

The two tables below give the input and the six skipped states. The diagrams label only the states cap[i, j]. The board heights, water heights, widths, and capacities in the table follow from the input heights and the capacity formula.

frames.explanation: All six states have width less than 7, and the fixed left board limits the water height to at most 3. Their capacities are therefore below the recorded value of 21, so skipping them cannot miss the optimum. In state [0, 3], the right board (height 2) is shorter than the left. The water height drops to 2, the width is 3, and the capacity is 6. The water height is 3 in the other five states.
frames.title: All six narrower containers with the shorter left board fixed at i = 0 have capacity below 21

summary: Moving the left pointer inward from the shorter board changes the state from cap[0, 7] to cap[1, 7]. This skips six narrower states at once, all with left index 0 and right indices from 6 down to 1.

tables.caption: Six skipped states, with capacities calculated from the height array
